clue.text: Return to reality, as the jet set ultimately must

definitions.meaning: to stop daydreaming and face plain facts

definitions.text: as the jet set ultimately must
definitions.meaning: the jet set travel by air, and every flight ends by landing on the ground

explanation.surface: A remark that high-flying socialites must eventually face ordinary life again.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the idiom literally: people who live on jets must, at the end of each flight, physically land.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means abandoning fantasy for sober reality, and literally describes an aircraft landing.

clue.text: Quickly goes down and invests close to fourteen pounds?

parts.note: to sink money into something is to invest it
a stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds, so something weighing close to that is like a stone

explanation.surface: A question about someone putting nearly fourteen pounds into a falling investment.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British unit of weight equal to 14 pounds; 'pounds' tempts a money reading to go with 'invests'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something dropping straight to the bottom very fast, as a heavy rock does in water.

clue.text: Position involving work in the service of the army

definitions.text: Position involving work in the service of the army

parts.words: Position involving work in the service of the army
parts.note: reads like any military post, but 'service' also means a religious service, and this post is the clergy appointment to a regiment

explanation.surface: A job description for someone serving in the armed forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' does double duty in the reading: military service, and the church services this officer conducts.
explanation.definitionFit: The office of a clergyman attached to a regiment is a post whose work includes leading services for soldiers.

clue.text: Warship a short distance east, protecting Baltic port

indicators.note: the short distance surrounds the port as if guarding it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a foot is a short distance, abbreviated FT
Riga is the Latvian capital and port on the Baltic Sea
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A naval vessel stationed just east of a Baltic harbour to defend it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'protecting' means the foot surrounds the Latvian port as a guard would; 'a short distance' is a foot, not a mile or yard.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a type of fast naval warship, historically a sailing vessel and now an escort ship.

clue.text: Duck and another bird up in the air

parts.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, shaped like the letter O
a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: Two birds flying overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' is the cricket zero, O, rather than a bird, although 'another bird' invites that reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A question left unsettled is said to be undecided or unresolved, exactly like a matter still under discussion.

clue.text: Turbostar engine breaks down on the way home

indicators.note: an engine that breaks down falls apart, so the letters of the two words are reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Turbostar train's engine fails while it is travelling back to the depot.
explanation.walkthrough: A Turbostar is a class of British diesel train; 'breaks down' looks like the mechanical failure but signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Aircraft or vehicles heading back to their home station are described with this phrase, meaning homeward bound.

clue.text: Completely transferred between spinner and weaver

definitions.meaning: a top is a spinning toy, and Bottom is the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream, so something passed from one to the other went between those two

explanation.surface: Thread passing completely from the spinner to the weaver in a textile mill.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick Bottom is the weaver in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream; the spinner is a top, the spinning toy, not a person spinning yarn.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means entirely or thoroughly, as when a house is cleaned in every part.

clue.text: Craftsman finishing as European monarch

parts.note: Polish describes someone from Poland, a European country
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A craftsman putting the final touches on work as a European king.
explanation.definitionFit: A worker who gives wood or metal its final smooth, glossy finish is a craftsman finishing the job.

clue.text: Literary form of essay by American author

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe was an American writer
to essay is to attempt or try

explanation.surface: Asking what literary form an American writer's essay takes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'essay' is the verb meaning attempt, not a piece of prose, despite 'Literary' beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse is a literary form, the art of writing in metre and rhythm.

clue.text: Feel better in republic, having power without king

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside, so the republic goes around the king

parts.note: Peru is a South American republic
K is the chess abbreviation for king
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: Someone recovering their spirits in a republic now that power is no longer with a king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside, so PERU encloses K to make PERKU.
explanation.definitionFit: To brighten up or recover spirits after feeling low is to become cheerful and lively again.

clue.text: A game of cards and a couple of drinks — goodness!

parts.note: gin is one spirit
rum is a second spirit
my! is an exclamation of surprise, like goodness!

explanation.surface: Cards, a couple of drinks and a cry of surprise make an evening.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a well-known card game for two players in which sets and runs are collected.

clue.text: Blackbird in wood

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
an owl is a bird

explanation.surface: A blackbird sitting in a wood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blackbird' splits as black + bird. In the game of bowls, a lawn game, the balls are called woods.
explanation.definitionFit: In lawn bowls each ball is traditionally called a wood, since they were once made of lignum vitae.

clue.text: Strike, perhaps, that brought parts of this island together

definitions.meaning: a strike is an action taken by a trade union, an example of a union's deed

definitions.text: that brought parts of this island together
definitions.meaning: the 1707 and 1800 laws joined England with Scotland, and Great Britain with Ireland

explanation.surface: A strike that once unified the regions of Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The Acts of Union of 1707 united England and Scotland into one kingdom on the island of Great Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally the phrase is a deed done by a trade union, such as a strike; as a title it names the uniting legislation.

clue.text: Game to imprison bitter, twisted pirate

indicators.note: one piece locks the other inside it, as a cell holds a prisoner

parts.note: footer is old British slang for football

indicators.note: the word for the drink is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: bitter is a type of British beer

explanation.surface: A pirate who has locked up bitter that went off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twisted' reverses the drink, and 'to imprison' locks it inside the game; footer is dated British schoolboy slang for football, and bitter is a British beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A buccaneer who plunders for loot, from the Dutch for booty-seeker, is another word for a pirate.

clue.text: Problem about family following a tortuous course

indicators.note: the problem goes around the family, enclosing it

parts.note: a snag is a problem or hitch
kin are one's family

explanation.surface: A family problem winding on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: Winding in curves like a serpent is moving along a twisting, tortuous path.

clue.text: Central principle king's not kept in view

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: the word not is held inside the view

parts.note: an eye is a view, as in keeping an eye on things
taken as written

explanation.surface: A ruler's central idea is not to be seen in public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kept in' puts the word not inside the view; 'view' is an eye, as in 'in the public eye'.
explanation.definitionFit: The fundamental theme or guiding idea of a speech or policy is its central principle.

clue.text: Rich pleasure-seeker, such as Ronnie Winslow?

definitions.meaning: a wealthy man devoted to having fun
Ronnie Winslow is the title character of Rattigan's drama The Winslow Boy, so he is a boy from a stage play

explanation.surface: Asking whether Ronnie Winslow was a wealthy hedonist.
explanation.walkthrough: The Winslow Boy is a Terence Rattigan play about a cadet, Ronnie Winslow, accused of theft; he is the boy of the play.
explanation.definitionFit: A wealthy man who spends his life chasing pleasure is a classic description of a hedonist man-about-town.

clue.text: But it's not a revolutionary society!

definitions.text: But it's not a revolutionary society!

parts.words: But it's not a revolutionary society!
parts.note: the name sounds like a group devoted to revolving, yet it is a respectable service organisation, not a band of revolutionaries

explanation.surface: An insistence that a certain society has no radical aims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' is meant as turning round, which the first word of the name means, not political overthrow.
explanation.definitionFit: This international service organisation took its name from rotating meetings among members' offices, hence the revolving joke.

clue.text: Instrument neighbour returned

indicators.note: turned back, so the word for neighbour is read in reverse

parts.note: to neighbour something is to abut it, lying next to it

explanation.surface: A neighbour gave back a borrowed instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neighbour' is a verb here, meaning to border on.
explanation.definitionFit: A large low-pitched brass wind instrument is a common example of a musical instrument.

clue.text: Players not at home in Selkirk, for example

parts.note: the players in a production are its cast
away means not at home, as in an away match

explanation.surface: Actors away from home touring in the Scottish town of Selkirk.
explanation.walkthrough: Selkirk looks like the Scottish Borders town, but it is Alexander Selkirk, the marooned sailor who inspired Robinson Crusoe.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Selkirk was marooned on a Pacific island for four years, making him a shipwrecked or marooned person.

clue.text: Bagpiper's short pibroch's beginning as lament

parts.note: wee is the Scots word for small, as a Scottish piper would say

indicators.note: the start of the word pibroch supplies just its opening letter

explanation.surface: A Scottish piper's brief pibroch opens as a lament.
explanation.walkthrough: A pibroch is a classical piece of Highland bagpipe music, often a lament.
explanation.definitionFit: To lament is to mourn or shed tears over something, so the verbs mean the same.

clue.text: Travels round the world with gold coins

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
bits are small coins, as in a threepenny bit

explanation.surface: A traveller going round the world carrying gold coins.
explanation.definitionFit: A satellite circles the globe, moving in a closed path around the planet.

clue.text: Caught moving in Act I right away

indicators.note: the letter for caught changes position within the phrase

parts.note: Act I is read as the words act one
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Someone caught in the act of moving during the first act of a play.
explanation.walkthrough: Shifting the C of ACTONE further along gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Immediately or without delay is the common meaning of both phrases.

clue.text: Went too far, getting excited on parts of test

indicators.note: one piece placed after the other, as if built on it

parts.note: a Test match in cricket is made up of overs of six balls each
hot means excited or passionate

explanation.surface: Someone getting worked up over sections of an exam and going too far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'test' is the cricket Test match, not an exam; its overs are the sets of six deliveries.
explanation.definitionFit: To miss a target by going beyond it, as a plane overshoots a runway, is to go too far.
